title: Introduction to Binary Search
description: Understand how binary search works on sorted data and how it reduces search time

blocks.text: One of the most elegant algorithms in computer science. Binary search finds an element in a sorted array by cutting the search space in half with every single step.
Suppose you need to find the number 37 in a sorted array of 1000 elements. Linear search checks one by one worst case, 1000 checks.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785405851844-125967514.png
Linear Search: Checks elements one by one, so with 1000 elements it may take up to 1000 checks (O(n)).
Binary Search: Repeatedly halves the search space, so with 1000 elements it takes only about 10 checks (O(log n)), but requires a sorted array.
The rule: Binary search only works on a sorted array. Sorting is the price you pay but once sorted, every search is blazing fast.
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
You keep three pointers left, right, and mid. At every step you look at the middle element and ask one question:

items: Is arr[mid] less than target? → target is in the right half, move left up
Is arr[mid] greater than target? → target is in the left half, move right down

blocks.text: Each question eliminates half the remaining elements. That's why it's O(log n).
Step by Step Find Target 23
Array: [3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31]  |  Target: 23
Step 1:  left=0, right=7, mid=3. arr[mid]=15. 15 < 23 → go right half.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785405851846-92862663.png
id=3 → arr[mid]=15 < 23 →move left to mid+1
Step 2: left=4, right=7, mid=5. arr[mid]=23. 23 == 23 → found!
mid=5 → arr[mid]=23 == 23 →found at index 5!
Only 2 steps to find the target in an 8-element array. For a million elements it would take at most 20 steps.
What if the Target is Not Found?
Array: [3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31]  |  Target: 10
Step 1: mid=3, arr[mid]=15 > 10 → go left half.
mid=3 → arr[mid]=15 > 10 →move right to mid-1
Step 2: left=0, right=2, mid=1. arr[mid]=7 < 10 → go right half.
mid=1 → arr[mid]=7 < 10 →move left to mid+1
Step 3: left=2, right=2, mid=2. arr[mid]=11 > 10 → move right to mid-1=1. Now left > right → stop.
left > right →target not found → return -1

items: Set left=0, right=n-1.These are the boundaries of your search space.
Loop while left ≤ right.When left crosses right, the target doesn't exist.
Compute mid = left + (right - left)  2.Never use (left+right)/2 it can overflow in other languages.
Compare arr[mid] to target.Equal → return mid. Too small → left = mid+1. Too big → right = mid-1.

blocks.text: The most common mistake:Usingwhile left < rightinstead ofwhile left <= right. That misses the case where the target is the last remaining element. Always use≤.
Find first occurrence of a value
When duplicates exist and you want the leftmost index, don't stop at the first match record it and keep searching left.
Search in a rotated sorted array
The array was sorted, then rotated at some pivot. One half is always sorted check which half and decide where to search.

blocks.text: The bigger idea: Binary search is not just for arrays. Any time you can ask "is the answer in the left half or right half?" you can apply binary search. This includes searching on answer ranges, not just arrays.
